job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Amira Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Amira, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying for a master's in cybersecurity at Norwell, and I share a student flat with a friend from my bachelor's. A normal day is a morning lecture on network defence, lunch with my study group, then a few hours in the lab running attack and defence exercises. I did a computer science degree, with one internship in a bank's IT team and one in a hospital's, where I mostly cleaned up old accounts. I like the puzzle of finding the hole before someone else does. What wears me out is that everyone assumes cybersecurity means hoodies and drama, when it's mostly checklists and patience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that makes sense and my phone will still autocorrect badly. At work I'd say let's use the tools that proved themselves and review them every year. To friends I'd say good, we get another few years to figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my plan holds. Finish the master's, join a security team at a bank or hospital, get a couple of certifications over three years. Attackers also use AI tools, so my field still has plenty to do, and I'd say that's true even in a plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at three kinds of employers: banks, hospitals and a consultancy. I'd start the first certification during the master's, since employers like seeing it. And I'd keep using AI tools occasionally for things like log summaries, with a human checking the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a steady road with a few bumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before you trust an AI tool at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where the data goes, who can see it, and whether it makes things up. In the hospital, we weren't allowed to put patient information into any outside tool, and that rule makes sense to me. So I'd ask the security team for the approved list, and I'd stick to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still worry you in this plateau picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Entry-level hiring, a little. Security teams are small, and a bank can only hire one junior at a time. My cushion helps, and my dad, who runs a tile shop, says he can cover me for a year, but I'd rather not need it.

To friends I'd say we get a few more years to **figure it out**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already happening, so let's plan. At work I'd ask the security team to list which tasks software now does, and who reviews them. Online I'd be quiet, but with friends I'd say the cautious ones will do fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the entry tasks in my field are exactly the thinking work the card says moves: alert triage, report writing, checking code for obvious holes. So a junior's role might be more about overseeing the machine than doing the work. That's a different job, and fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for a role that includes incident response, where you must act under pressure with people. I'd also start using AI tools more consistently, in a sandbox, to learn their limits. And I'd get a certification that employers still ask for, since it may help me stand out in a smaller pool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job looks reachable, but I think I'm in a good spot to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does being in a good spot mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm training on a changing field, I use tools once they're proven, and I can still wait a few months before applying. I'm not the first to move, but I'm not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whom would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The friends in my flat who are doing a generic IT degree. They're good, but their entry work is the help desk, which is the first thing a chatbot answers. I've told them to look at security or infrastructure, but not everyone wants to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's far too fast for banks, hospitals or governments to cope with. At the university I'd ask what the degree will be worth in 2028 and get nobody to answer. Online I'd add my voice to the call for a clear plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared the sums don't add up. Cybersecurity looks safe because attackers use AI, but defenders would be using it too, and a few experts could do what a whole team does. There'd be fewer seats, and I'd be a graduate with no track record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the slow route and take whatever security job I can, even a help-desk-with-security-duties one, so I'm inside an organisation. I'd put my savings into an index fund only after I've kept six months in cash. And I'd ask my dad whether I can help in his tile shop if I have to, which isn't glamorous but is solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not paralysed, but I can't pretend it's anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the master's still worth it in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the first half is. I'd probably take a placement mid-year instead of finishing all of it. Knowledge matters, but a name on a team matters more when everyone's fighting for few seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad in that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I may need to stay at his place and help in the shop for a while. He'd say of course, but he'd look worried, because he paid for part of my degree. I'd tell him that your job isn't what you studied, it's what you can do when things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something about it, if we're not lazy. I'd tell my friends to build skills that need judgement and trust, since that's what a security person sells. And I'd tell the university to teach us how to supervise AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel nervous but have a plan. By 2031 I'd be 29, with five years of security experience, hopefully in a role where I'm responsible for decisions. The risk is that a smaller team can handle what a bigger one did, so I'd need to be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and join a security team at a hospital or a bank. I'd spend years two and three on incident response, and I'd learn AI tools alongside colleagues so I'm not late. I'd also save a quarter of my pay in case of a lull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a tight window, but a clear one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the five-year picture different from the two-year one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not rushing. With two years I'd take the first job and worry about the rest later, but with five I can pick a place where I'll be taught properly. That makes the tool question a question of habit, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does being the one they keep mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means being the person who's calm at 3 a.m. when something breaks, who writes the clear note afterwards, and who knows what the AI tool can't be trusted to do. A tool can't take responsibility, and a team will always want someone who can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to build the checks and the laws. I'd tell friends this is a chance to pick a field with long-term demand. And I'd say the people who'll do best are the ones who stay curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. By 2036 I'd be 34, maybe leading a team, with plenty of experience on real incidents. I'd worry more about the world's safety than my job, because attacks get cheaper too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work my way up in a security team, and add a certification every couple of years. I'd try new AI tools when colleagues have, not before. And I'd save for a flat and, perhaps, a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade is long enough to learn from my mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the world's safety?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That attacks become cheap. A person with no skill could rent an AI that finds holes in a hospital system. Then the defenders have to be faster, and that's where I come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And would that be a source of work for you, or a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. It's work, and I'd feel needed, but it's also a world where more people get hurt if a hospital goes down. I'd want to be on the side that keeps the lights on.

The people who do best will be the ones who stay **curious**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one. Hospitals and banks move slowly, and two years isn't enough for them to put the checks in place. What would help is a clear plan from employers about how many juniors they'll keep, honest advice on which certifications still count, and rules on where data can go. A bit of public money for training would also be good, as long as it's not just for big firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe just that I'm not as calm as I sound. I plan things because I don't like surprises, and the 2-year picture is mostly surprises. I'd rather someone told me the unpleasant bits now, in a table, than have me find them later.

headlineQuote: I plan things because I don't like surprises, and the 2-year picture is mostly surprises.
portrait: Amira is 24, doing a **master's** in cybersecurity at Norwell, with a bank and a hospital internship behind her.
She is a pragmatic centrist who uses **AI tools** now and then, and only ones that have proved themselves.
Her father runs a tile shop and could cover her for a year, giving a strong cushion.
She stays calm when the road is clear, and turns anxious when there is **no time to plan**.
Her bet is on responsibility: someone has to **answer** when systems break.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because banks and hospitals can't build checks in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Employers stating how many **juniors** they'll keep, and honest advice on certifications.
Public money for **training** that doesn't only go to big firms.
